questions.q: 1 a) State the formula for Binomial distribution. [L1][CO3] [2M]
questions.a: If X is the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials, each with success probability p and failure probability q = 1 - p, then X follows a binomial distribution. Its probability mass function is P(X = x) = nCx * p^x * q^(n-x), for x = 0, 1, 2, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is npq. It is a discrete distribution used when there are a fixed number of independent trials with only two possible outcomes per trial.
questions.explanation: Each of the x successes contributes p and the remaining n-x trials contribute q; the factor nCx counts the number of ways to choose which trials are successes. Independence of trials allows the probabilities to be multiplied.
questions.oneShotPreview: Binomial: P(X=x) = nCx p^x q^(n-x); mean = np, variance = npq.

questions.q: 1 b) A coin is tossed 9 times. Find the probability of getting 5 heads? [L1][CO3] [2M]
questions.a: Here n = 9 trials, p = 1/2 (head) and q = 1/2 (tail), so X ~ Binomial(9, 1/2). P(X = 5) = 9C5 * (1/2)^5 * (1/2)^4 = 126 / 2^9 = 126/512 = 63/256. Therefore the probability of getting exactly 5 heads is about 0.2461 (24.61%).
questions.explanation: A fair coin gives equal success/failure probability, so the answer reduces to the number of favourable arrangements (9C5 = 126) divided by the total 2^9 = 4096 equally likely outcomes.

questions.a: The Poisson distribution is a discrete probability distribution that gives the probability of a given number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time, space, or volume when the events occur independently and at a constant average rate λ. Its probability mass function is P(X = x) = e^(-λ) * λ^x / x!, for x = 0, 1, 2, ... . Both the mean and the variance of the distribution equal λ. It is often used as an approximation to the binomial distribution when n is large and p is small.
questions.explanation: It models rare, random, independent occurrences such as the number of defective items or incoming calls, where only the average rate λ is known. The single parameter λ completely determines the distribution.
questions.oneShotPreview: Poisson: P(X=x)=e^-λ λ^x/x!, modelling random events; mean = variance = λ.

questions.q: 1 d) If the variance of a Poisson variate is 3. Find P(1 ≤ X < 4) ? [L1][CO4] [2M]
questions.a: For a Poisson distribution, variance = mean = λ, so λ = 3. We need P(1 ≤ X < 4) = P(X=1) + P(X=2) + P(X=3). Using P(X=x) = e^-3 * 3^x / x!, this is e^-3 (3 + 9/2 + 27/6) = e^-3 (3 + 4.5 + 4.5) = 12 e^-3. Since e^-3 ≈ 0.049787, the probability is 12 * 0.049787 ≈ 0.5974.
questions.explanation: The Poisson variance equals its parameter, fixing λ = 3; summing the three integer probabilities in the interval gives the required range probability.

questions.q: 1 e) State Normal probability density formula. [L1][CO4] [2M]
questions.a: A continuous random variable X with mean μ and standard deviation σ is normally distributed, written X ~ N(μ, σ²), with probability density function f(x) = (1 / (σ sqrt(2π))) * exp[ -(x - μ)² / (2σ²) ], for -∞ < x < ∞. The curve is bell-shaped and symmetric about x = μ. The standard normal distribution has μ = 0 and σ = 1, with z = (x - μ)/σ.
questions.explanation: The density integrates to 1 over the real line; the exponent measures the squared distance from the mean, giving the characteristic symmetric bell shape controlled by σ.

questions.q: 2 a) Derive mean of Binomial distribution. [L3][CO3] [5M]
questions.a: Mean E[X] = Σ_{x=0}^{n} x * nCx * p^x * q^(n-x). The x = 0 term is zero, so E[X] = Σ_{x=1}^{n} x * n!/(x!(n-x)!) * p^x * q^(n-x). Cancelling x with x! gives x * nCx = n * (n-1)C(x-1), hence E[X] = np * Σ_{x=1}^{n} (n-1)C(x-1) * p^(x-1) * q^(n-x). Putting y = x-1, the sum becomes Σ_{y=0}^{n-1} (n-1)Cy * p^y * q^((n-1)-y) = (p + q)^(n-1) = 1 by the binomial theorem. Therefore E[X] = np.
questions.explanation: The factor x nCx is rewritten as n(n-1)C(x-1), leaving a complete binomial expansion that sums to 1, so only np remains.
questions.oneShotPreview: Mean of Binomial, E[X] = Σ x·nCx p^x q^(n-x) = np.

questions.q: 2 b) 20% of items produced from a factory are defective. Find the probability that in a sample of 5 chosen at random (i) one is defective (ii) P(1 < x < 4) [L1][CO3] [5M]
questions.explanation: Each item is an independent Bernoulli trial with defect probability 0.2; applying the binomial pmf and summing over the requested values gives the two probabilities.

questions.q: 3 Fit a Binomial distribution to the following frequency distribution: x: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; f: 2, 14, 20, 34, 22, 8 [L3][CO3] [10M]
questions.a: Total frequency N = 100. Mean = Σfx/N = (14 + 40 + 102 + 88 + 40)/100 = 284/100 = 2.84. Since mean = np with n = 5, p = 2.84/5 = 0.568 and q = 0.432. Expected frequency = N * 5Cx * p^x * q^(5-x). The fitted frequencies are: x=0 → 1.5, x=1 → 9.9, x=2 → 26.0, x=3 → 34.2, x=4 → 22.5, x=5 → 5.9 (total ≈ 100). These are close to the observed frequencies, so the binomial fit with p = 0.568 is reasonable.
questions.explanation: Fitting means equating the theoretical mean np to the observed sample mean to estimate p, then using the binomial pmf scaled by N to generate expected counts for comparison.

questions.q: 4 a) Out of 800 families with 5 children each, how many would you expect to have (i) 3 boys (ii) 5 girls (iii) either 2 or 3 boys. Assume equal probabilities for boys and girls. [L3][CO3] [5M]
questions.explanation: Equal boy/girl probabilities make all 2^5 = 32 birth sequences equally likely; multiplying each probability by 800 gives the expected number of families.

questions.q: 4 b) Two dice are thrown five times. Find the probability of getting 7 as sum i) At least once (ii) P(1 < x < 5) [L1][CO3] [5M]
questions.explanation: Each throw of the dice is an independent trial with success probability 1/6; the complement rule handles 'at least once' and direct summation handles the strict inequality range.

questions.q: 5 a) Derive mean of Poisson distribution. [L3][CO3] [5M]
questions.a: For X ~ Poisson(λ), E[X] = Σ_{x=0}^∞ x * e^-λ * λ^x / x!. The x = 0 term vanishes, so E[X] = e^-λ * Σ_{x=1}^∞ x * λ^x / x! = e^-λ * Σ_{x=1}^∞ λ^x / (x-1)!. Factor out λ: E[X] = λ e^-λ * Σ_{x=1}^∞ λ^(x-1) / (x-1)!. Let y = x-1; then the sum is Σ_{y=0}^∞ λ^y / y! = e^λ. Hence E[X] = λ e^-λ * e^λ = λ. Thus the mean of a Poisson distribution is λ (which also equals its variance).
questions.explanation: Cancelling x against x! and shifting the index leaves the exponential series, so the entire sum collapses to the single parameter λ.
questions.oneShotPreview: Poisson mean: E[X] = Σ x·e^-λ λ^x/x! = λ.

questions.q: 5 b) If 2% of light bulbs are defective. Find the probability that (i) 2 defective items (ii) at least 3 defective items (iii) P(2 < x < 5) in a sample of 100. [L1][CO3] [5M]
questions.explanation: With large n and small p the Poisson approximation is appropriate; the mean λ = 2 drives all three probability calculations.

questions.q: 6 Fit a Poisson distribution to the following data: x: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, Total; f: 142, 156, 69, 27, 5, 1, 400 [L3][CO4] [10M]
questions.a: Total N = 400. Mean = Σfx/N = (156 + 138 + 81 + 20 + 5)/400 = 400/400 = 1, so λ = 1. Expected frequency = N * e^-1 * 1^x / x! = 400 * e^-1 / x!. Using e^-1 ≈ 0.3679, the fitted frequencies are: x=0 → 147.2, x=1 → 147.2, x=2 → 73.6, x=3 → 24.5, x=4 → 6.1, x=5 → 1.2 (sum ≈ 400). These closely match the observed frequencies, confirming a good Poisson fit with λ = 1.
questions.explanation: For a Poisson fit the sample mean estimates λ; multiplying the pmf by N gives expected counts that can be compared directly with the given frequencies.

questions.q: 7 a) An insurance agent policy of 5 men all of identical age and good in health. The probability that a man of this age will be alive 30 years is 2/3. Find the probability that in 30 years. (i) At least one-man (ii) Atmost three will be alive [L1][CO4] [5M]
questions.explanation: Each man's survival is an independent Bernoulli trial with p = 2/3; the complement rule gives 'at least one' and direct summation gives 'at most three'.
questions.oneShotPreview: n=5, p=2/3: P(at least 1 alive)=0.9959; P(at most 3)=0.5391.

questions.q: 7 b) If X is a Poisson variate such that 2P(X = 0) = P(X = 2) find (i) Mean (ii) P(2 < X ≤ 5) iii) P(X ≥ 3). [L1][CO4] [5M]
questions.explanation: The given relation determines λ from the Poisson pmf; all requested quantities then follow by substituting λ = 2 into the pmf and summing the relevant terms.

questions.q: 8 If X is a normal variate with mean 30 and standard deviation 5. Find i) P(26 ≤ X ≤ 40) and ii) P(X ≥ 45) [L1][CO4] [10M]
questions.explanation: Standardizing converts the normal variable to Z ~ N(0,1), and standard normal table areas give the required interval and right-tail probabilities.

questions.q: 9 In a sample of 1000 cases, the mean of certain test is 14 and standard deviation is 2.5. Assuming the distribution to be normal find (i) How many students score between 12 and 15 (ii) How many students score above 18? (iii) How many students score below 8? [L3][CO4] [10M]
questions.explanation: After standardizing, each probability is an area under the standard normal curve; multiplying by the sample size converts the proportion into an expected number of students.

questions.q: 10 If the masses of 300 students are normally distributed with mean 68kgs and standard deviation 3kgs. How many students have masses i) Greater than 72kgs ii) Less than or equal to 64kg iii) Between 65 and 71 kgs inclusive. [L3][CO4] [10M]
questions.a: μ = 68, σ = 3, N = 300, with Z = (X - 68)/3. (i) z = (72-68)/3 ≈ 1.33, so P(Z > 1.33) = 1 - 0.9082 = 0.0918, giving about 28 students (27-28). (ii) z = (64-68)/3 ≈ -1.33, so P(Z ≤ -1.33) = 0.0918 by symmetry, again about 28 students. (iii) z = -1 and +1 for 65 and 71 kg, so P(-1 ≤ Z ≤ 1) = 2(0.8413) - 1 = 0.6826, giving about 205 students.
questions.explanation: Standardizing each mass to a z-score lets us use symmetry and standard normal areas; multiplying by 300 converts each proportion into an expected count.

questions.q: 11 If p is probability of getting head in tossing a coin and a coin is tossed 12 times then Find P(3≤X≤6) using i) Binomial distribution ii) Normal distribution. [L3][CO4] [10M]
questions.a: Assuming a fair coin, p = 1/2, q = 1/2, n = 12. (i) Binomial: P(3≤X≤6) = (12C3 + 12C4 + 12C5 + 12C6)/2^12 = (220 + 495 + 792 + 924)/4096 = 2431/4096 ≈ 0.5935. (ii) Normal approximation: μ = np = 6, σ = sqrt(npq) = sqrt(3) ≈ 1.732. With continuity correction, P(2.5 < Y < 6.5) gives z = -2.02 and 0.29, so P = Φ(0.29) - Φ(-2.02) ≈ 0.6141 - 0.0217 = 0.5924, which closely agrees with the exact binomial result.
questions.explanation: The exact binomial sum is compared with the normal approximation (using the continuity correction); both agree closely because np and nq exceed 5, validating the approximation.
questions.oneShotPreview: Fair coin: Binomial P(3≤X≤6)=0.5935; Normal approx ≈0.592.
